passage:
Simran, come sit. Your Maria Aunty wasn't always calm about this sort of thing. In Class 9 there was a boy, Dinesh, who took my lunch and laughed at my glasses. I was terrified to tell anyone, because I was sure he would find me after school. For a month I said nothing, and my stomach hurt every morning.
Then our school put a complaint box outside the office, no name needed. I dropped in a note with the dates. I walked to the gate with two friends for weeks, never alone. And I let the principal and my parents deal with him. I never faced him myself.
My fear was reasonable, Simran. It never meant I shouldn't tell.

qa.q: What did the school put outside the office?
qa.a: The school put a complaint box outside the office, where no name was needed.

qa.q: Why did Maria stay silent for a month?
qa.a: She was terrified that Dinesh would find her after school, so she was afraid of what he would do if she spoke.

qa.q: What could Simran do if afraid a bully will get back at them?
qa.a: Simran can use an anonymous route like the box, stay with friends instead of alone, and let adults handle the danger.

qa.q: How might the principal have seen the note in the box?
qa.a: The principal probably saw it as a chance to learn about the problem and act on it without exposing the student who wrote it.

grounding: An elder recalls fear of a bully's retaliation and how an anonymous note, staying in a group and letting adults act kept her safe.

passage:
Dear Nirmala Didi,
You asked why I've been so quiet on our calls. It's a boy in Class 12 who's been taking the juniors' lunch money behind the gym and slapping anyone who says no. Last week he saw me watching and said, 'Say a word and you're next.'
I've been scared every single day. I wanted to tell Sir, but what if he found out it was me?
Then I remembered what you said about the anonymous box outside the counsellor's room. So on Tuesday I wrote down everything, the place, the times, the boy's name, and dropped it in without my name. I also told Amma, and she said I was right to be scared and right to report.
Now I walk to the bus with Kunal and his brother, never alone. Today the counsellor and the vice principal stood behind the gym all lunch. Nobody went near it.
I'm still nervous. But it feels like the grown-ups are carrying it now, not me.
Hrithik

qa.q: Where did Hrithik put the written report?
qa.a: In the anonymous box outside the counsellor's room, without a name.

qa.q: What was Hrithik feeling after the boy's warning?
qa.a: Hrithik felt scared every single day, afraid of being next if the report was traced.

qa.q: Which steps kept Hrithik safer while still reporting?
qa.a: Using the anonymous box, telling Amma, and walking to the bus with Kunal and his brother instead of alone.

qa.q: How might the juniors feel seeing adults behind the gym at lunch?
qa.a: Relieved and safer, since adults were now handling the danger.

grounding: A letter from a teen afraid of a bully's retaliation who uses an anonymous report, stays in a group and lets adults handle the danger.

passage: People think telling is easy. It isn't. I'm Arohi, and last year a girl in Class 11 decided I was her target. Pushing my tray, hissing things on the stairs, and once: 'If you go crying to anyone, I'll make it worse.' I believed her. For a month I said nothing. Then Sahil, my lab partner, noticed I was taking the long staircase every day and asked why. I told him, and he said, 'You don't have to put your name on it.' He was right. Our school has an online form where you can report without your name. I filled it in that night, with dates and places, while Mumma sat next to me. After that I made sure I was never alone on the stairs; Sahil and two others walked with me. Within a week the girl was called in with her parents. The teachers handled it. I never had to face her. Being scared was sensible. Staying silent wasn't.

qa.q: What did the girl say would happen if Arohi told anyone?
qa.a: 'If you go crying to anyone, I'll make it worse.'

qa.q: Why did Arohi stay silent for a month?
qa.a: Arohi felt frightened and believed the threat that things would get worse.

qa.q: What made reporting feel possible for Arohi?
qa.a: The school's anonymous online form, Mumma sitting alongside, and friends walking together on the stairs.

qa.q: How did Sahil notice something was wrong?
qa.a: He saw Arohi taking the long staircase every day and asked why, showing he was paying attention.

grounding: A spoken account of a teen afraid of a bully's retaliation who reports anonymously, stays with friends and lets teachers handle it.
